title: Common Scanner Mistakes
summary: Identify, debug, and prevent the top 6 Scanner bugs: skipped newlines, InputMismatchException, premature close, and loop re-instantiation.
learningObjectives: Diagnose and fix InputMismatchException when reading mismatched data types
Prevent premature stream closure bugs where scanner.close() permanently disables System.in
Avoid memory leaks and buffer desynchronization caused by re-instantiating Scanner in loops
Use hasNextX() methods defensively to validate input before consumption
expectedOutcomes: Debug crashing console programs without panic by reading stack traces
Write robust, fault-tolerant CLI applications that handle bad user keystrokes gracefully

activities.title: The Top 6 Scanner Bugs & How to Fix Them

breakdown.whatIsIt: A diagnostic survey of the six most frequent runtime errors and logic bugs when reading console input.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Understanding error causes transforms hours of frustrating trial-and-error into immediate 5-second fixes.
howItWorks: hasNextInt() previews the input token before parsing to prevent exceptions.
Single Scanner instance maintains a coherent buffer state across loops.
System.in is a JVM singleton; closing any scanner attached to it terminates terminal reading.
keyTakeaways: Use hasNextInt() or try-catch to prevent InputMismatchException crashes.
Never instantiate Scanner(System.in) inside a loop.
Closing a scanner closes System.in permanently for the entire application.
Clear leftover newlines with scanner.nextLine() after reading numbers.

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: Crash-Proof Menu Loop
activities.description: Notice how this program prevents crashes: it checks hasNextInt() before calling nextInt(), discards bad input with scanner.next(), and closes the scanner only once at program termination.

questions.prompt: What compiler error occurs if you use Scanner without importing java.util.Scanner?
questions.explanation: Because Scanner is in java.util, omitting the import makes the symbol 'Scanner' unknown to the compiler, producing 'cannot find symbol: class Scanner'.
hints: The compiler cannot locate the class definition.

questions.prompt: What happens if a user inputs 'abc' when your code executes scanner.nextInt() without hasNextInt()?
options: It ignores 'abc' and waits for a number
questions.explanation: Scanner throws InputMismatchException when the available token does not match the expected integer pattern.

questions.prompt: Why is creating 'Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);' inside a while loop considered an anti-pattern?
options: It is illegal Java syntax and will not compile
It repeatedly allocates heap objects and can lead to buffering desynchronization bugs
Scanner can only be used once per JVM lifetime
questions.explanation: Repeatedly instantiating Scanner creates unnecessary garbage collector overhead and risks buffered characters being lost between instances.
hints: Think about memory efficiency and buffer consistency.

questions.prompt: What happens if you close a Scanner that wraps System.in, and then later try to create a new Scanner(System.in) and read from it?
options: It throws NoSuchElementException or IllegalStateException because System.in remains closed
It reads from the computer's microphone instead
questions.explanation: Closing a Scanner closes its underlying stream (System.in). The JVM does not allow standard I/O streams to be reopened once closed.
hints: Closing a wrapper closes the underlying source stream forever.

questions.prompt: How does calling scanner.next() inside an else block help after a failed hasNextInt() check?
options: It converts the bad token to an integer
It consumes and removes the invalid token from the buffer so the program can move on
questions.explanation: hasNextInt() only checks the token without removing it. If you don't call scanner.next() to consume the bad token, it stays stuck in the buffer and loops indefinitely.
hints: You need to discard the bad token to unblock the buffer.

questions.prompt: Why does typing '25.0' into scanner.nextInt() throw an InputMismatchException?
options: 25.0 contains a decimal point, making it a floating-point literal which cannot be parsed as an int
It is a bug in the Java language
questions.explanation: nextInt() strictly requires characters matching integer digits. Even if the fractional part is .0, the decimal point causes the integer regex to fail.
hints: A decimal point is not an integer character.

questions.prompt: What happens if you type '100L' when scanner.nextLong() is called in the console?
options: It throws InputMismatchException because 'L' is not a digit
questions.explanation: The 'L' suffix is for Java source code literals. User console input must contain only numeric digits; typing 'L' triggers an InputMismatchException.
hints: User input should not include Java source code suffixes.

questions.prompt: If a method throws NoSuchElementException on scanner.next(), what is the most likely cause?
options: The input stream reached End-Of-File (no more tokens are available)
The user typed a number too fast
questions.explanation: NoSuchElementException is thrown when scanner attempts to read a token but the stream has no more tokens (e.g. redirected input file reached EOF).
hints: It means 'no element exists to read'.

questions.prompt: How can you read numbers in European format (e.g. '3,14' instead of '3.14')?
options: It is not possible in Java
questions.explanation: Scanner is locale-sensitive. Changing the locale via scanner.useLocale(Locale.GERMANY) configures it to parse decimals with comma separators.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to handle user input when you cannot predict whether the user will type an integer or text?
options: Always call nextInt() and hope for the best
Read the input as a String using nextLine() and validate/parse it programmatically
questions.explanation: Reading everything as a String via nextLine() never throws InputMismatchException. You can then inspect the string or parse it with try-catch.

questions.prompt: What happens if you execute scanner.close() twice?
options: Nothing, closing an already closed Scanner has no further effect
questions.explanation: The close() method on Scanner is idempotent; calling it on an already closed scanner has no effect.
hints: Idempotent operations can be repeated safely.

practice.title: Defensive Integer Input Validator
practice.problemStatement:
Write a complete Java program in the Main class that prompts the user for an integer.
• If the user enters a valid integer, print: Valid number: [n]
• If the user enters invalid text, print: Error: Invalid integer format

Use hasNextInt() defensively to prevent InputMismatchException.
hints: Always close the scanner at the end.

activities.title: Top Placement Interview Questions: Scanner Debugging

interviewQA.question: What is the danger of closing a Scanner wrapping System.in inside a helper method?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `scanner.close()` invokes `close()` on the underlying `InputStream` (`System.in`). Standard input is a process-level resource. Once closed, any subsequent attempt to read from `System.in` anywhere else in the application will fail with a `NoSuchElementException` or `IllegalStateException`. In utility helper methods, never close a Scanner wrapping `System.in`; manage its lifecycle in `main()`.
keyPoints: Closing System.in prevents any further terminal input across the entire JVM lifecycle.

interviewQA.question: How do hasNextInt() and nextInt() interact during user input?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `hasNextInt()` evaluates the next token against the integer regex without advancing the Scanner's position or consuming the token. If valid, calling `nextInt()` immediately afterwards consumes that exact token. If `hasNextInt()` returns false, the invalid token remains at the head of the buffer and must be consumed with `scanner.next()` to unblock subsequent reads.
keyPoints: hasNextInt() inspects without consuming; nextInt() consumes the token.

interviewQA.question: Why does typing '12.5f' in terminal input cause an InputMismatchException for nextFloat()?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In Java source code, `12.5f` tells the compiler to treat the decimal as a 32-bit float literal rather than a 64-bit double. However, user input at runtime represents data, not source code. Scanner's regex parser expects digits and an optional decimal point; the letter `'f'` is considered an invalid character, throwing `InputMismatchException`.
keyPoints: Literal suffixes ('f', 'L') are compiler tokens, not valid runtime numeric characters.

interviewQA.question: Why is Scanner considered not thread-safe?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `Scanner` is not synchronized. If multiple threads access the same `Scanner` instance concurrently without external synchronization, their buffer positions and token extraction will race, leading to corrupted input reads and unpredictable `NoSuchElementException` errors.
keyPoints: Scanner methods are not synchronized; do not share a Scanner across multiple threads.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between NoSuchElementException and InputMismatchException?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `InputMismatchException` is a subclass of `NoSuchElementException`. It is thrown specifically when a token is available in the stream, but cannot be parsed into the requested type. `NoSuchElementException` is thrown when no tokens are available at all (e.g. End-Of-File reached).
keyPoints: InputMismatchException = token exists but wrong type; NoSuchElementException = no token exists.

interviewQA.question: How can you discard an entire bad line of input after a failed validation?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Call `scanner.nextLine()`. This reads and discards all remaining characters on the current line including the trailing newline, effectively resetting the buffer to the beginning of the next line.
keyPoints: Call scanner.nextLine() to purge an entire malformed line from the buffer.

interviewQA.question: Is try-with-resources recommended for Scanner wrapping System.in?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Generally NO for `System.in`, because try-with-resources will automatically call `scanner.close()` upon exiting the block, permanently closing `System.in`. However, for file-based scanners (`new Scanner(new File(...))`), try-with-resources is strongly recommended to guarantee that file handles are released.
keyPoints: Try-with-resources is ideal for file scanners, but risky for System.in if subsequent input is needed.

interviewQA.question: Why does a while(scanner.hasNext()) loop fail to terminate in the console?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Because `System.in` remains open indefinitely waiting for more keyboard input. The console never sends an EOF (End-Of-File) signal during normal typing unless the user explicitly presses `Ctrl+D` (on Linux/Mac) or `Ctrl+Z` (on Windows).
keyPoints: Console streams do not send EOF automatically; while(hasNext()) waits indefinitely.

interviewQA.question: How does scanner.useDelimiter() help when reading comma-separated user data?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: By calling `scanner.useDelimiter(",")` or `scanner.useDelimiter("[,\\s]+")`, you can tell Scanner to split tokens by commas and whitespace rather than whitespace alone, enabling instant CSV record parsing.
keyPoints: useDelimiter() customizes token separation for formats like CSV.

activities.title: Topic Confidence Checklist
checklist: I know to import java.util.Scanner at the top of my file.
I know how to prevent InputMismatchException using hasNextInt().
I avoid creating multiple Scanner instances inside loops.
I understand why closing System.in prematurely breaks future inputs.
I never type 'L' or 'f' suffixes when entering console values.
